“What’s going on here? New training exercises?” Phainon asked in half-jest as he surveyed the chariot race and spectators. 

“Some friendly competitions in Strife’s honour. A Kremnos tradition.” 

“Competitions? Yet you’re not participating?” 

“The host is responsible for overseeing the games and allocating the prizes.”

“Well… what about me?” 

“What about you?”

He smiled so earnestly Mydei was torn between averting his gaze or doing something unwise to wipe it from his mouth. “May I participate? It’s so lively here. The rousing cheers, the spark of competition—I’ve been reeled in.”

Slowly, Mydei blinked and tilted his head but Phainon’s bright visage was unchanged. 

Upon the anniversary of Castrum Kremnos’ fall at his own spear, in the shadow of Okhema’s high walls, Mydei hosts the annual funeral games—a celebration of glory and mourning bound up in Strife. It’s an old tradition frowned upon by the city the Kremnoan legion has come to unwillingly inhabit. But a necessary one.

This year, for the very first time, Phainon wishes to participate.
notes_html: So I took one look at my copy of the Iliad on my shelf, remembered the funeral games was A Thing, and decided it fit so perfectly into Kremnoan culture that this fic possessed me until it was completed.

chapters.html:
Hooves thundered and wheels rattled across the plains beyond Okhema’s high walls. Kremnoan shouts roared in the wake of racing chariots: cheers when their favourite overtook first place now fallen to second, insults when their favourite lost control of their horses and steered off an advantageous course, and foul language all around. 

Safe but caged within the Holy City, these words and emotions were suppressed into something more acceptable to those who looked down upon Kremnoans and their traditions. They were scorned as brutish and blood-thirsty. Unfit for civilised company. Never mind that Mydei had heard far worse within Dawncloud’s assemblies. 

The rough curses were too much for the more sensitive ears within the city, always attentive for the slightest Kremnoan tendency to critique, but were loosed like lit arrows upon the plains where the low grass and upturned soil would contain their outburst. 

The lead charioteer was a woman, Iole, who had accompanied Mydei in exile. Her age had begun to show in streaks through her dark hair but her judgement was as sound as it had always been. Her horses were swift but led by her steady hands as they hugged the turning post so tight there were bound to be wheel marks along the dead stump. 

A betting pool was too distasteful for this kind of event. If there were one, Mydei had no doubt she would be the overwhelming favourite to win. 

Second place was more unexpected. Telys had been a boy when his family followed Mydei from Castrum Kremnos to Okhema but he had grown into a young man and capable charioteer. His youth showed in his riskier strategies. 

Unwise manoeuvres, as some would call it. Beside him, Krateros had scowled when Telys squeezed between the tree line and another chariot, and threatened to upend them both. If this were battle then Mydei would agree with the sentiment. For today, he respected the ambition. 

“There you are!”

The figure shuffling through the jostling crowd was at home within the white, sun-bleached stones of Okhema’s streets but appeared a stranger amidst the Kremnoan legion. Too many clothes, features too boyish, and an obvious confusion behind his bright smile. 

Mydei checked on the chariot positions—Telys had rounded the post unscathed—and waved Krateros away to make space at Mydei’s side, otherwise devoid of his warriors who knew to give him a wide berth while at work, rest and play. Everyone knew such a thing without being told; it was sculpted into his unyielding body and stringent face that pushed Kremnoans to bow their heads and Okhemans to avert their eyes.

Obvious to all except one. 

“Deliverer,” Mydei greeted with a small nod. 

Phainon chuckled. “Good morning, Mydei. I searched all your usual haunts with nothing to show for my efforts. Who could have known you would be all way out in Okhema’s outskirts.”

“Who told you?” Mydei asked but there was only one person who could be responsible.

His smile turned sheepish as he scratched the back of his head. “Aglaea.”

Mydei had specified, as he had every year, that the Kremnoan detachment would be unavailable for the day. Himself included. Unless the black tide erupted from the ground beneath Kephale’s feet and knocked the Dawn Device from their shoulders, any issues reserved for the detachment would be pushed to tomorrow at the earliest. 

Yet Aglaea considered Phainon as exception to his demands that the legion remained undisturbed for the day. Worse, the intuition of the Romance demigoddess was never wrong. Anyone else would have been immediately dismissed from the grounds but he welcomed Phainon to his usual place at his side. 

“What’s going on here? New training exercises?” Phainon asked in half-jest as he surveyed the chariot race and spectators. 

Mydei, too, returned to the race. The distance between Iole and Telys had closed significantly. It was a close. “Some friendly competitions in Strife’s honour. A Kremnos tradition.” 

Phainon’s brows rose with his voice, “Competitions? Yet you’re not participating?” 

“The host is responsible for overseeing the games and allocating the prizes.”

Understanding smoothed out all but the last vestiges of his confusion. “Well…” His head swivelled around the crowd. Then he pointed at his chin. “What about me?” 

Mydei squinted. “What about you?”

He smiled so earnestly Mydei was torn between averting his gaze or doing something unwise to wipe it from his mouth. “May I participate? It’s so lively here. The rousing cheers, the spark of competition—I’ve been reeled in.”

Slowly, Mydei blinked and tilted his head but Phainon’s bright visage was unchanged. 

The opportunity to answer ended with a fresh bout of cheers and curses. Mydei broke away from Phainon’s gaze and returned to the chariot race. Telys had overtaken Iole and crossed the finish line first by less than a wheel’s width. 

Mydei motioned over the attendants; all children too young to participate, so hovered upon the elevated platform at the crowd’s edge so they could witness the event’s over heads of adults whilst within close proximity for Mydei to call upon. 

He spared Phainon a glance. “If you truly mean those words, remain here.”

Rather than more jest or prodding goad, Phainon’s smile softened. “All my words to you are honest and heartfelt, Mydei.”

“Right.” 

He could easily challenge that notion with a mental list of every outrageous thing Phainon had ever spouted at him. Instead, he turned away and his skin, from the tips of his ears to his shoulders, prickled with heat that could be waved off as the consequence of sun exposure from dawn to midday. 

The reward for the chariot race’s victor was a ritual silver tripod bearing the image of Nikador and Castrum Kremnos’ high walls. Contrary to his wild charioteering, Telys accepted the tripod with light hands and a soft smile too weighty to be considered gentle. 

His dazed expression and the silver gleaming in his enlarged pupils were a reverence for an old, mad god and a long forsaken homeland. One that existed only in the distant memories of a child and the stories spoken by those around him—memories mixed with myths. 

Mydei moved on to present Iole with a thoroughbred mare yet to be broken. Then distributed the rest of the rewards, from a bronze cauldron untouched by the fire to a simple string of coins. The victors and losers took the results with grace and an unspoken promise to claim the position above theirs in the year to come. 

The legion flocked together in long lines. Shoulder square and chins back, they waited for him to proclaim the next competition and its spoils with the same discipline as their practiced military formations.

In front of them all, Phainon waited beside Mydei with a poorly concealed eagerness, a dog wagging its tail. They could all see for themselves that Phainon had arrived for whatever reason, but any bafflement was silenced in wait of Mydei’s explanation or dismissal of the topic.

“Warriors of the Kremnoan legion! Okhema’s Deliverer wishes to participate in our games!”

Phainon lifted his hand in a small wave and, if this were the marketplace or bathhouse, Mydei would have rolled his eyes. As it were, this was a public spectacle of which Mydei was the host. He had standards. 

Despite the proposition of a foreigner, an Okheman in all but birth no less, there were none of the objections Mydei had expected. It may as well have been warm approval. 

There was some sense to it. Mydei had never been covert about Phainon’s status—as a fellow Chrysos Heir, as a comrade, as an equal. It was plain for them all to see after a duel of ten days and ten nights that played out in reduced scale every time they shared the training grounds—and Phainon had gone on to earn their respect directly when he accompanied the detachment on expeditions. 

Besides, this was a day of competitions. Who better to measure oneself against than the best: the Deliverer. 

Still, he had expected some hesitance. 

Phainon was already watching, awaiting the verdict, when Mydei smirked at him. “The price of your entry shall be the foot race. If you wish to participate in the rest of the day’s events then you must outrun at least one of the three fastest Kremnoans.”

Phainon’s lips curled into the same smirk, eyes narrowed, head tipped at an angle that shed the boyish swell of his cheeks for something sharper, almost devious. “Challenge accepted.”

A thrill raced through him, heating his blood so quick his mind lost its tether and he almost forgot the purpose of all this. He couldn’t compete but, for the first time since he began this tradition, he wanted to. Wanted so badly he clenched his teeth to hold it down. 

He announced the prizes and the rules, sending out a small group of attendants to mark a closer turning post than the chariot race. Meanwhile the warriors sorted themselves into spectators and willing competitors and prepared themselves. 

Beside him, Phainon prepared with some light stretches. His coattails brushed the earth as he leaned to stretch his calves. 

Mydei’s hand twitched but he crossed his arms. “Shed some of that modesty. Before you complain upon the results that you were disadvantaged.” 

Phainon straightened up. “Have you no faith in me, Mydei? I’m hurt,” he complained yet unfastened the belt across his chest to loosen his pauldrons. 

Mydei arched a brow at Phainon’s carefree grin. “What happened to those heartfelt words of yours?” 

In a flutter of dark fabric, Phainon’s blue chlamys landed in Mydei’s arms, followed immediately by his cumbersome white coat. Outside of the bathhouse changing stations, it was the first time Mydei had seen Phainon without his distinctive coat to leave only the shirt underneath. 

Most of it was already visible when the coat was overtop, and the floral pattern embroidered upon the white sleeves was the same as his coat sleeves—all Aglaea’s handiwork. 

The major difference was Phainon’s exposed forearms. The veins were stark in the strip of pale skin, stretched over taut muscles, between his short black gloves and sleeve ends. A view that only grew as he rolled up his sleeves up as far as they would allow.

Mydei’s scowled. “Find a proper coat hanger.”

“There are no trees nor rocks nearby,” Phainon retorted as blithely as he resumed his stretches.

Mydei already knew that because he had ordered the Kremnoans to clear the plains in preparation for the very first year of games. The soil was packed down afterwards and left to recover until careful maintenance throughout the year. 

“It would hardly be fair if I were forced to run in search of a convenient place to store my belongings. Aglaea’s golden threads surely extend this far, and I doubt she’d appreciate me throwing those items into the trodden soil,” Phainon finished with that earlier smirk returned in full.

It was a daring expression so removed from the beloved hero of the Amphoreus, they were almost two entirely different people. One given to the people and the other reserved for Mydei. 

“Yet you feel the need to run your mouth.” 

He snarked but tucked the decorative chlamys under his arm and folded the coat first so he could bundle it into the chlamys. He would prefer to personally keep ahold of any belongings Phainon had entrusted to him rather than hand them off to an attendant. 

It was too inconvenient to hold so he tossed it onto the ornate seat prepared every year for Mydei, though he rarely sat in it. Phainon kicked off his shoes and lined them up beneath the seat. 

The turning point had been marked and the competitors arranged themselves at the starting line. Although Phainon had removed his outermost layer, there was no denying he was overdressed compared to the others. Everyone else wore a suitable exomis and set of sandals easy to remove for events where extra fabric slowed them down and sandals risked injuring their ankles. 

Yet Phainon ran quicker than any of them. Stable footing, perfect posture, unwavering balance even where the ground bumped and dipped. His core, thighs and calves were strengthened from years of wielding a greatsword that others, warriors and civilians alike, struggled to lift let alone swing. 

That immeasurable strength carried forward into his effortless sprint. When Phainon ran, a white blur across the grassy plains, he made it look as easy and natural as the sunlight streaking over the horizon. Never mind the gap between him and his so-called competition. 

There was only one other person in Mydei’s memories who ran in such a way—with the wind at their back and beneath their feet. It had earned him the position of Mydei’s messenger, and even he would fail to compete with Phainon.

He rounded the turning post and returned to the starting line, now finish line, while second place was only three quarters of the way through the race. 

The Kremnoan congratulations were scattered with barely audible praises in common tongue but Phainon understood the sentiment. Face flushed, dripping sweat from his brow down his collars neck to his heaving chest, he smiled and accepted their commendations that came in words and pats upon his back. 

His sleeve had unravelled during his sprint, leaving it loose for a warrior to tug on it, mouth moving with words Mydei couldn’t hear as he frowned from a distance. Phainon failed to hear either considering he leaned down for her to speak in his ear. She pointed and he followed it into the crowd, then nodded.

She lifted her arm with a shout of someone’s name. Another warrior broke from the others with a kylix in both hands and doused Phainon over the head with water. He ran a hand through his drenched hair, tossed his head back and laughed to the skies like he could make the sun shine brighter upon him by virtue of the clear, clean sound. 

He still didn’t quite belong but it was a near thing. Much nearer than Mydei had expected, despite Phainon sharing blood and iron with the Kremnoan warriors on the battlefield against the black tide. Of course, if any of Okhema’s citizens could bridge the gap between the holy city and the refugees of its age old enemy, it would be Phainon. 

No matter the crowd Phainon inserted himself into, the audience he stood before, he managed to win more than their approval but their adoration. He understood what they wanted and moulded himself into the shape they would hold in their eye and hands. 

The Kremnoans were no exception. Mydei was exempt only because he would dig his gauntleted fingers into the cracks if Phainon even attempted to shift, flowing like clean waters to nourish the city’s heart, into something more palatable. To hide as something empty. 

As the other runners finished up, the legion dispersed to offer their congratulations elsewhere and Phainon was free to weave his way back to Mydei’s side. 

“I won,” he announced, as though Mydei could have looked away while he claimed victory like a child plucked fresh flowers from the earth, and now presented them at Mydei’s feet. 

It was a futile effort but Mydei waved a square of cloth at him. “Congratulations. It was an overwhelming victory.” 

No one stood a chance. Not unless Mydei had kicked off his sandals and offered Phainon a real challenge. 

Phainon dabbed at his forehead, absorbing almost nothing before it was replaced by the drops from his bangs. “What was my prize? A silver krater?” 

“You misunderstood. The foot race was to test your ability and resolve,” Mydei reminded him. “You were a participant. Not a competitor.” 

Phainon paused as he digested Mydei’s words. Once he did he chuckled under his breath. “Semantics. You almost sounded like a council member on Dawncloud.” 

His nose wrinkled. “Save your insults for your own ignorance.” 

“So my prize is being a true competitor in the other events,” Phainon mused, still uselessly swiping at his damp cheeks rapidly cooling from their heated hue. “Or did I misunderstand you again.” 

“You’re correct. This time.” 

“Great!” 

He went to dry his neck but he glanced at the saturated cloth with great consideration.  The intent was clear upon his face. 

“Deliverer…” Mydei began his warning. 

Before Phainon shook himself off like a dog. Water speckled Mydei’s skin and garments as it was flung from the ends of Phainon’s hair and dewy skin. 

He shielded his face behind his hands and scowled. “You!” 

Phainon laughed. “It’s only some water. You looked…” He dragged his eyes down Mydei’s face to the swell of his chest and further to his abdomen, dropping his voice with it. “A little warm.” 

He walked around almost bare compared to the modest dress sense of Okheman’s who wavered between gawking and averting their eyes. Yet this was the first time he felt exposed for it.

He certainly did not look warm. The same way his body naturalised poisons, blood loss, and injuries, temperature and sun exposure had little effect on him unless they were at their extremes.

There were no eyes on them. Everyone was too preoccupied with the other runners. 

“Then fetch me some water,” Mydei drawled and Phainon’s eyes widened, glittering like sunlight through the same water droplets he had scattered everywhere, “instead of shaking it onto me like a misbehaving mutt.” 

Phainon’s throat bobbed around a swallow, water glistening off his golden sun tattoo, and his lips parted to reply but nothing more than a thin exhale escaped him. 

It was time to distribute the prizes for the foot race, so Mydej stepped around him with one more command, checking no one was watching when he murmured into his ear, “Stay.” 

A much better behaved dog, a hunting hound Mydei had trained himself, was the reward for second place while third received a small cauldron. The victor was awarded a kylix from the detachment’s days of wandering. 

It had accompanied Mydei for many years longer than the person it once belonged to. But he still recalled how the wine had drained from it as fast as the owner’s feet crossed great distances. 

The next competition was spear throwing. Unsurprisingly, with his impressive arm strength—which had earned him third place in Okhema’s arm wrestling competition. Second or first were beyond his means solely because he had to forfeit to Castorice—Phainon’s spear soared over the empty plains into the surrounding woodlands. 

It forced Mydei to announce a rule amendment: an extra victor for every event Phainon chose to participate in, and Phainon would receive new prizes chosen from Mydei’s storehouse. A Chrysos Heir’s blood was naturally a boon above those who bled the red of mortals rather than the gold of the gods.

Not to say that Phainon’s dominance over the competition was due to birthright alone. Even if he bled like a mortal without connection to the Titans, he would have been a strong contender in every category through his sheer dedication and ambition. 

The prize for first place was an untouched cauldron best suited to brewing decoctions. It was a shame the item would be passed down without the previous owner’s knowledge. The cauldron would more likely be used for cooking than the work of a physician.

Next was the archery competition. The warriors drew lots to determine who would loose their arrow first. In Castrum Kremnos, the target would have been a timid dove tied by the foot to a post, but Mydei had long switched it to a stuffed scarecrow. The deadlier the precision, the greater the score. 

Phainon was one of the last to shoot. With his upper body strength, he would have no difficulty drawing back the heavy bow. However, unless throwing his great sword to decapitate a Titankin lumbering towards a downed warrior sufficed, Mydei had never seen Phainon demonstrate long range precision. 

Both of them were close range combatants, Mydei with his fists or a spear and Phainon with his greatsword. All their spars had revolved around drawing first blood or pinning the other to the dirt rather than aim. 

In his youth, the detachment had taken turns teaching how to wield their own weapons, so there were few he could be presented with that he couldn’t brandish at a reasonable skill level. Although frowned upon for the sake of combat as cowardly, the bow had value on the battlefield and the hunting grounds. 

Phainon’s form was promising: feet balanced apart, back straight and shoulders squared. One continuous line that flowed from his head past his trim waist to his feet. 

His back muscles straining through the black fabric of his shirt, skin tight even before it was dampened by sweat, with the sheer effort of holding the bowstring taut. Yet his breaths and arms were steady. He didn’t appear like a novice, who would have loosened their arrow too quick under the strain. He was unwavering—as was his aim. 

It pierced through the scarecrow’s head. Even if the warrior, embodied in straw, had donned a helmet, Kremoan arrows were forged to pierce armour. The arrow was undeniably lethal. As deadly as if the arrow had shot through Mydei’s own tightened chest while he watched Phainon wipe his brow and smile like it was nothing. 

The first prize was an ivory aulos. It was well cared for, hardly a scuff on its pale surface, because its owner had preferred string to wind instruments. The lyre in particular, which left their voice free to intertwine with the notes resonating through the air. 

“You never boasted your skills in archery,” Mydei said once the spoils had been distributed. 

Phainon shrugged as he nibbled on a small loaf slathered with goat’s cheese, gathering energy for the next event. “I wasn’t aware I had any.” 

Eagerly indulging in his light snack, he didn’t elaborate. 

“What?” Mydei demanded answers. 

“I observed the other competitors and copied them,” Phainon explained, as though it were obvious.

Simple rather than terrifying. He had loosed a perfect arrow through the forehead as a novice whilst giving the impression of a master.

He knew Phainon was intelligent—capable and adaptable. Enough to earn Aglaea’s faith despite her stringent standards, and graduate from the Grove of Epiphany while learning Okheman’s political landscape and his new role as the Deliverer—but it felt different when Phainon’s prowess came in the form of a potentially dead man at the hands of an unfamiliar weapon. 

The day’s final event was a boxing competition. Phainon stripped off his black shirt to expose the defined ridges of his back, especially his shoulder blades as he folded the garment and laid it with his others. He had a clear view of the scars decorating his skin like awards of his valour. Not to mention the clean cut of his surprisingly small waist Mydei could measure with his hands. 

Phainon’s first opponent was immediately evacuated to the Twilight Courtyard with a dislocated jaw and potential concussion. One good swing to their jaw had whipped their head so quick Mydei anticipated the resounding crack of their neck. Fortunately they slumped to the ground in a heap, unconscious rather than dead.

It would be an offence for a warrior to restrain their strength against another, even in friendly competition. An insult so grave the slighted warrior could demand a chance to restore their honour through a duel to the death. 

Phainon knew enough to give his full swing every time. Some opponents were swift-footed but Phainon tracked their movements with the same narrowed eyes he used against black tide creatures. Other opponents were sturdier, although rarely as large as Phainon himself, and could endure a hit or two. He struck them down all the same. 

The results were entirely expected. Mydei sparred with Phainon frequently, sometimes every day multiple times a day, before Phainon dragged Mydei to the bathhouse to relax their aching muscles. Phainon’s capabilities and his limits were as ingrained into Mydei’s mind and body, both to strike in a spar and to guard on the battlefield, alongside his own. 

When Mydei presented the reward for first place, the boxer’s eyes were still watery and dazed from Phainon’s jab that crooked his nose. Another patient for the Courtyard but much less urgent than the unconscious bodies Phainon had left in his wake. 

Hyacine always had much work this time of year but she never complained, or even frowned. Mydei would need to provide her another gift in thanks this year. Perhaps two with the greater influx of patients at Phainon’s hands. 

The highest prize was a bronze shield. The craftsmanship was intricate but the designs of Nikador’s wings over a fiery battlefield, meant to rouse the wielder’s courage and strike fear into their opponents, did nothing to detract from its toughness. 

The scuffs and minor dents each bore a story that Mydei could recite by heart—close his eyes and relive it in memory. It had been struck by arrows, swords, spears when raised to his defence by the warrior who had been most worthy to fight alongside him. 

The end of the competitions was marked by a ritual ceremony to Nikador. Surrounded by lit touches, roiling with the flames of war, Mydei stood behind a gold ceremonial tripod. One supposedly forged from the crowns of past kings who had fallen to Kremnos, engraved with the image of the Strife Titan, and set aflame for the duration of the games. 

The Kremnoan detachment raised their kylixes in toast and Mydei did the same. Within his own should have been the blood drained from a slitted ox at the foot of Nikador’s altar. Instead it was spiced pomegranate honey brew, within the traditions set by Phagousa’s intervention, that Mydei poured into the tripod to douse the flames. 

“In Strife’s name, grant eternal glory and honour to those who came before us. And those who will come long after!”

The Kremnoan detachment poured their libations, soaking into the earth like blood after a long battle. They roared like thunder to split the sky and travel to distant lands where Castrum Kremnos lingered on.

In place of Nikador’s ceremonial flame, the warriors lit several bonfires to gather around. Alongside the spiced wine, the fires brought warmth to the evening, as though such a thing as night still existed to stave off. In distant lands where even the day and night were outside their grasp, the familiar bonfires kept them in good company. 

This part of the festivities held little interest to him. As the host he was obligated to stay while the others exhausted their worries by daylight and drank the rest of them away by supposed nightfall. 

Today… 

Mydei flicked his finger and beckoned Phainon, once again fully clothed, to follow him away from the bonfires. Today Mydei could escape early under guise of providing Phainon the rewards he had earned, as any proper host should.

The guards at the city gates had been forewarned about the detachments activities and knew to wave them through without trouble. While Mydei and Phainon would never encounter any such difficulties, one word from his detachment members about any prejudices and the guards would be scheduled for a disciplinary hearing.  

“Where are we going?” Phainon whispered. He was so close to Mydei’s heels, almost shoulder to shoulder despite Mydei leading while he followed, that he didn’t need to raise his voice any louder. “We passed your storehouse.” 

They were in the Kremnoan district, devoid of any sleeping citizens to be so considerate on. All of them were celebrating outside the city walls. 

Still, Mydei murmured back, forcing Phainon to lean over his shoulder to hear him. “These items are stored in my home.” 

“Taking me home?” His warm breath broke against Mydei’s ear as a teasing lilt and he suppressed a shiver. He spared Mydei when he abandoned that tone for one of curiosity, “What were you all celebrating? A festival to Nikador I presume.” 

“Of a kind.” They were close to his home and he quickened his pace. “The events were all funeral games.” 

“Oh. I see,” Phainon said, carefully neutral. 

The confusion wasn’t unfounded. Okheman funerals were more somber, subdued affairs and the funerals of Phainon’s hometown, wherever that was, were no doubt similar in nature. 

But glory was at the centre of Kremnoan life. From birth to death, living was the pursuit of glory. In name, in spoils, in a legacy that would persist after death. In the honour of being welcomed to an eternal battlefield in the afterlife while immortalised in the minds and songs of comrades within the living realm. 

As the Titan worshipped by Kremnoans, Nikador embodied Courage, Tenacity, Sacrifice, Reason and Honour. There was an existence born from competition, a concept that encompassed events as great as war and conquest, and as ordinary as a game of knuckle bones. The Kremnoans lived to follow in their wake. 

It should be no surprise that fallen warriors were honoured with a ceremony of Strife. 

As they entered his street, he explained, “No one perished. These funeral games mark the anniversary of Castrum Kremnos’ fall.” 

Many warriors had perished during that battle—the first time in its thousand year long dynasty that Castrum Kremnos’ walls had been breached. Whether the exiles of the detachment or the citizens of Kremnos, everyone who came to join Mydei in self-imposed exile once the blood and dust settled had lost someone. Including himself.

In Okhema, the funeral games were seen as barbaric practices that disrespected the life of the deceased. Too raucous, too self-centred, too violent. The same as all Kremnoan traditions, they were looked down upon with a derision felt by the people who clung to them in connection to a homeland they had been forced to flee.

As tensions simmered and threatened to boil over in the early years of their settlement into the city, Mydei had discussed the idea of the funeral games with Aglaea. The events were exhilarating, rewarding, a test of resolve and ambition. They were also an emotional outlet, akin to lifting the lid before a pot could boil over. 

Mourning for comrades who had fallen in the battle for Castrum Kremnos and in scattered battlefields during the past year. Frustrations over the culture forcibly suppressed within the city. A longing for home.

Phainon stood beside him on the doorsteps as Mydei unlocked his door. “Anniversary? So may I participate again next year?” 

Mydei paused. He wouldn’t have faulted Phainon for shying away from the event after learning its true meaning. As always, his words were sincere, bright yet more subdued and grounded. 

Oblivious, Phainon continued with a small chuckle. “It was a lot of fun. I can see the appeal of being celebrated this way. Instead of tears, those you care for can rally together, blood pumping and heart racing, and smile.” Just as Phainon smiled at him, small but all the more earnest for it. “I enjoyed it, Mydei.” 

If it was what Phainon truly wanted then Mydei wouldn’t deny him. Just one question remained: 

“Why did you come looking for me?” 

It was an annual event in which Mydei and the detachment disappeared from the city, yet this was the first time Phainon had sought him out rather than wait for his return. 

“Oh.” Phainon laughed to himself again, a little foolish and self-deprecating as he scratched his cheek. “I figured there was a reason you didn’t invite me to whatever you had planned but… you looked sad. You always do this time of year.” 

Why was Phainon embarrassed by the admittance? The heat beginning to colour the swell of his cheek should be Mydei’s to feel when it was his emotions that had apparently been on such clear display all these years. Ones he thought hidden by stoicism, smothered by duty, reduced to a small, sharp blade to prick himself on while nobody noticed. 

Apparently someone did notice. Of course it would be Phainon. 

Mydei swiftly unlocked his front door and snagged Phainon by the strap of his coat. He yelped as Mydei dragged him over the threshold, slammed the door shut, and pinned Phainon against it to kiss him breathless. 

Phainon’s head jerked away on instinct and crashed into the door but, when Mydei began to pull away to ask if he was alright, Phainok grabbed the back of his neck and hauled him back in. 

It was clumsy. A bit messy. Their heads tipped the wrong way and their noses bumped together. Their rhythm was less a push and pull, and more of neither knowing what to do with themselves. Proof that their relationship was still somewhat new. In this, and perhaps only this, Phainon was neither experienced nor an audaciously fast learner. 

But Mydei had waited all day for the privacy to do exactly this. All the while Phainon teased him, deliberately and unintentionally, with sultry words and looks, with his prowess and his body on full display like a bird fanned their feathers. And Phainon’s feathers had been particularly beautiful, almost enough to make Mydei forget himself. 

So he pressed Phainon into the door and let his desire bruise their lips and steal their breath away. 

His lungs burned, spreading fire through his body and heating his blood until he was dizzy. The only reason they broke apart was Phainon’s hand seizing his hair to drag him back. 

The scant air between them was warm, wet, with their pants. Phainon’s swollen lips turned glossy with the swipe of his tongue over them, darkened eyes peering at Mydei through his lashes. 

“Finally,” he rasped. Not as breathless as Mydei wanted but close. “I wanted to do that since I saw you. Is this my prize?” 

It was the most breathless he had sounded all day. A foot race and boxing tournament was nothing but one kiss and he was panting, rasping, flushed red. 

Mydei was the same. Both of them reduced to such a state because Mydei had suggested they keep their relationship private for now. Before the weight of public expectation, of the Deliverer, of the Crown Prince, could crush whatever was between them before they had the chance to nurture it into something as strong as they were expected to be. 

Phainon pouted and tugged his hair, not away but to grasp his attention. “I won more competitions than one. Don’t be stingy, Mydei, I deserve more.” 

Mydei’s huffed a laugh as his head bowed, breaking eye contact so he had a chance to compose himself. “Haikas,” he chided, too soft and affectionate to be a true insult. “I have a real reward for you.” 

He untangled them and invited Phainon to make himself comfortable in the andron while he fetched something from his storeroom. Out of all the rooms in the house, this one had been the most carefully selected. 

The least daylight so he could easily filter out the rest with thick window covers. No draughts or chance of infestation. Sufficient space for shelves and mounts of all sizes because all of these items, carefully dusted and gleaming with their routine polish, meant more to him than a storehouse that proved the glory he had earned and didn’t care for. 

Empty spaces were scattered throughout and each had been filled the day prior. Leonnius’ beautiful silver kylix, Perdikkas’ untouched medical cauldron, Peucesta’s aulos, and Hephaestion’s shield. Today, they had all been passed onto worthy champions. 

One of Ptolemy’s original scrolls from the Library of Garbaniphoro was meant to join the other prizes. In the end, he had been unable to part it. The memories of Ptolemy teaching a feral boy—more creature than human once dredged from the Sea of Souls—to read had ached too much. Perhaps next year. 

All these items were the vestiges of the people, dear companions, who held a special place in his heart. There would be pieces that would never leave him but every year, in the days leading towards the funeral games, he locked himself in the storeroom. 

There he relived his memories of the past in the same way his people reminisced for Castrum Kremnos. The city had meant little to him, a mere bastion meant to be conquered for revenge, for justice, because home had meant wandering the wilds of Amphoreus with the detachment and his companions. 

It was where he learned to read and write, to wield a spear and any number of other weapons, experienced the highs and lows of battle, of victory and loss. 

He basked in natural sunlight that descended into night and returned again. He breathed fresh air from the vast forests and mountain peaks. He relived battles where both disappeared beneath the smoke of war.  

Then decided what he was ready to let go of. Not because his companions were losing their place in his heart, but because his heart had grown with the world he had come to inhabit and he refused to let himself remain chained to the past when he wanted to prove there was a path forward for them all. 

He didn’t need a kylix, a cauldron, an aulos, a shield to tell him what his friends meant to him, back then and even now. He already knew—beneath all the bruises and scar tissue that was slowly beginning to heal. To be healed. 

Nestled in silk upon Hephaestion’s shelf, the item he chose to linger on today was one he thought he would never part with. Yet he didn’t doubt himself as he lifted both items from their cushions and wasn’t that proof of how far he had come? 

By the time he returned to the andron, Phainon had snuck off to the kitchen, pantry, and back again to recline on a kline. The food was laid out on the table: a platter of nuts and another of dried figs, a dish of pomegranate seeds, all accompanied by chalices of pomegranate juice mixed with goat’s milk rather than wine. 

He had reclaimed his clothes after the last event and redressed himself in the proper clothes of Okhema’s Deliverer. Yet his expression didn’t belong to the amiable hero, nor the mettlesome warrior of the games. It was too soft, too subdued, in a way Phainon rarely let himself exist because there had to be—he had to be, as they both did—something that others could see and hold fast to. 

He gazed out the window, so lost in his thoughts it was simple for Mydei to enter the room on silent, bare feet and come up behind him without drawing attention. 

Mydei laid a golden crown of laurels atop Phainon’s head. 

Rather than shed his relaxed state in a moment of surprise, Phainon only tipped his head back, hand lifting to his head. Upside down as he met Mydei’s eye with a silent question. 

Hand cupped beneath his neck, Mydei coaxed his head upright and straightened the laurel wreath. It suited him: the same gold of his eyes and the accents of his clothes. If not for the baffled crease of his brow and downturned lips, there would be a regal air to him. 

“It’s one of your prizes,” Mydei said, voice surprisingly steady for what he was about to do. “This is the other.” 

From Mydei’s hand, an earring dangled in a slip of daylight that glinted off a blue jewel set in gold. 

Both items were commissioned for Hephaestion. Although Mydei wasn’t a king, hardly a prince no matter how the others chose to venerate him and his connection to their homeland, he had wished to honour Hephaestion as his dearest companion. 

There was no king and no Kremnos Festival, but Mydei had intended to elevate Hephaestion to his King’s Aegis.

No more than an adolescent, Hephaestion had seen the truth before Mydei could even offer and rebuffed him without hesitation. 

“With this sickly body of mine, I can hardly consider myself worthy of such a place at your side. But know this, Mydeimos, one day you shall meet a warrior your equal who you can entrust with your back.” 

It wasn’t graceful but Mydei had accepted Hephaestion’s refusal. The laurel wreath and earring had gone unused. 

A golden wreath because the King’s Aegis shared in the weight of the one true victor’s crown. 

An earring because the King’s Aegis was the king’s match, their shield and their spear, their shadow and their partner, their other half as needed. 

Most importantly, the earring was made to appear a pair with Mydei’s own. Even if Phainon couldn’t see the rest of the meaning embedded deeper than the faceted jewel and shaped gold, he could see that much. 

His gaze flitted between him and the earring, uncertain as he murmured, “Mydei…”

Phainon was still down to the breath stalled in his lungs as Mydei cupped his chin and held the jewellery to his right ear. More gold, and a blue that matched his eyes. As though the pair belonged to Phainon and he had bestowed one upon Mydei as a gift rather than this way around. Mutual belonging and possession. 

This thing that brought pain, by sight, by touch, like a well-worn blanket too threadbare to keep him warm through the winter yet he sought comfort in it anyways—now it made him smile. “It suits you. Wear it often.” 

His ear would need to be pierced first, so there was no use in holding it up. Mydei went to set the earring aside but a hand snatched his wrist before the distance between them could grow. 

“Mydei, wait,” Phainon demanded, near begged, as his eyes darted across Mydei’s face. Lost but searching for a way through. “Does this mean…” 

When Mydei suggested they keep their relationship a secret, it had been phrased as a question and Phainon had agreed.

Now, his hopeful eyes but thinned lips afraid to be wrong were proof of what Mydei had already suspected—he made a mistake. Of course he had agreed. Because Phainon would take what he was given without asking for more. 

It had been foolish of Mydei to think it was for the best. It wasn’t himself he had underestimated—the Kremnoans followed him like thunder followed the lightning from Nikador’s lance. The Council of Elders and most vitriolic Okhemans had spat at him before and they could do so again if they chose—it had been Phainon. 

Phainon who had lost his home once and longed for another. Who gave bits and pieces of himself away with love and didn’t expect any back but quietly yearned for it. 

The Okhemans would never turn on him but the Kremnoans had begun to warm up to the warrior who shared their poor rations, their flimsy tents, their battle wounds, and Mydei hadn’t wanted to take that away from him. 

Except Phainon was his equal. It wasn’t Mydei’s decision to make. 

His lip curled, crooked smile growing, a smirk, joy and mirth and challenge stirred into one as he leaned closer. “Next time, if you want something from me, take it.” 

No matter when and where. 

They were so close, Mydei could witness the realisation spread through the unknowing twitch of Phainon’s expression. Understanding chased by joy as his eyes creased and he grinned; visible for the brief moment before he grabbed Mydei by his necklace and yanked him into a kiss. 

Mydei’s hands gripped Phainon’s waist that had tormented him since he removed his long coat in the early afternoon. Phainon held him in turn, one arm wrapping around his torso and the other his neck. 

This time, they fell faster into a comfortable position, the same rhythm, and pulled away in sync. 

Phainon nestled their foreheads together and the gold looked especially radiant against his coloured cheeks. “Not a bad prize.” 

Mydei scoffed. “Feel free to relinquish it if you have no desire for it.” 

“I never said that,” Phainon drawled, unhurried when they both knew Mydei’s words were empty.  “I’ll put it to good use.” 

“It would be a waste otherwise,” he agreed and let Phainon pull him into another kiss. 

A shorter one as Phainon ended it to say, “We both still need to bathe. Want to kiss in the Hero’s Bath?”

“Aglaea will have us removed from the premises,” Mydei rebuked. She already lectured them on their bath competitions, he didn’t want her to add public indecency to the end of it. 

“Marmoreal Marketplace,” Phainon suggested instead. “The rooftop.” 

“Shameless,” Mydei chastised but didn’t object. 

Not when Phainon was on his feet in an instant, hand tangled with Mydei’s so he could tug him towards the front door and into the city streets where anyone could see them. Not even when Phainon, shimmering wet and golden across his pale skin, kissed him in the Hero’s Baths until a Garmentmaker appeared with a threatening rap of its sword against the tiles. 

Certainly not once they were on the rooftop above Marmoreal Marketplace, sharing the same blanket, the same air, the same strip of daylight, while Mydei toyed with Phainon’s earlobe. Tomorrow, once Mydei pierced Phainon’s ear himself and clipped gold and blue into place, that earring would shine in the daylight where it belonged.
